newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries open higher before jobless claims.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries open higher before jobless claims.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries opened higher on Thursday in front of weekly jobless claims data and September personal income and spending figures.
The 6-3/4 percent 30-year bond was up 6/32 to 100-24/32, yielding 6.69 percent.
The two-year note was up 2/32 at 100-6/32, to yield 5.77 percent.
"There's buying on dips," said Kevin Flanagan, first vice president and money market economist at Dean Witter Reynolds.
"Treasuries rebounded overnight after modest buying in Tokyo," said Kim Rupert, economist at MMS International.

Flanagan said while the market gets jobless claims data, personal income and spending figures and the Chicago Purchasing Managers (PMI) index today, it would probably take its cues from jobless claims and the Chicago PMI.

The Commerce Department releases September personal income and consumption at 0830 EST/1330 GMT. Economists surveyed by Reuters offered an average forecast of 0.6 percent growth in personal income and 0.3 percent growth in personal spending. In August, the prior month, each was up 0.6 percent.
Simultaneously, the Labor Department will release its jobless claims data for the week ended October 26. In the last report, jobless claims totaled 320,000.
Economists said the jobless data could feel some effects from the now concluded GM strike in Canada, which resulted in the idling of nearly 20,000 GM workers in the U.S.
Local strikes against General Motors Corp. in Wisconsin and Indiana that began this week would not show up yet in the jobless claims figures being reported today.
At 1000 EST/1500 GMT, the market will get the Chicago Purchasing Managers report (PMI).
Economists expect an October Chicago PMI reading of 54.0, down from 56.3 in September.
The National Association of Realtors will also release its third-quarter home affordability index at that time.
Housing data released on Wednesday indicated that higher interest rates have cooled housing activity, but not by much.

Despite the data being released today, analysts said much of the market's attention will still be focused on Friday's releases, which include the influential monthly payroll employment report and later, the October National Association of Purchasing Management's (NAPM) index.
Economists estimate that October payrolls grew by 2120,000 jobs in October after losing 40,000 jobs in September.
The NAPM index is expected to read 51.0, off a bit from 51.7 in September. A reading above 50 indicates that the economy is expanding. A reading below 50 points to slowing economic activity.

Should the employment data on Friday be stronger than expected, however, the 30-year bond yield would probably tread back up to 6.80 percent, thanks to the rally earlier this week which pushed Treasuries into a different trading range, said Flanagan.
"You've dropped the trading range, especially on the bond," said Flangan.
In early trade, three-month bill rates were down 1/32 to five percent, six-month rates were unchanged at 5.08 percent and year-bill rates down two basis points to 5.15 percent.
Five-year notes were up 3/32 to 100-18/32, yielding 6.12 percent.
The 6-1/2 percent ten-year note was up 5/32 to 100-26/32 to 6.39 percent.
-- North American Treasury Desk, 212-859-1679
